title: 1  Sets
text:
Theorem 1.1 (Cantor’s Theorem) For any set \(S\), \(|S| < |\mathcal{P}(S)|\).


Proof. We show that there is no surjection \(f : S \to \mathcal{P}(S)\).
Notice that we are essentially mapping \(S\) to subsets of \(S\). Then we just need to construct a subset of \(S\) that is not mapped to, given our mapping \(f\).
Let \(E := \{x \in S : x \notin f(x)\}\). This is a subset of \(S\), with the property that the elements in \(E\) are not in the subset of \(S\) that they are mapped to in \(f\). For every element in \(S\), we can check if \(e \in S\) is in \(E\) by seeing if \(e \in f(e) \subseteq S\).
We now show that there is no \(e \in S\) s.t. \(f(e) = E\), i.e. \(E \in \mathcal{P}(S)\) is an element of the codomain that is not mapped to:
Suppose for contradiction that \(\exists\, e \in S\) s.t. \(f(e) = E\). We check if \(e \in E\):
① If \(e \notin f(e)\), then by definition of \(E\), \(e \in E\). But \(E = f(e)\) so \(e \in f(e)\). \(\rightarrow\leftarrow\).
② If \(e \in f(e)\), then by definition, \(e \notin E\). But \(E = f(e)\) so \(e \notin f(e)\). \(\rightarrow\leftarrow\).
Thus, there is no \(e \in S\) s.t. \(f(e) = E\).
Then, \(f\) cannot be a surjection. \(\square\)

title: 2  Real Numbers
text:
Claim. There exists a unique positive \(r \in \mathbb{R}\) s.t. \(r^2 = 2\). Denote \(r\) by \(\sqrt{2}\).


Proof. Take the set \(A := \{x \in \mathbb{R} : x^2 < 2\}\).
We first show that \(\sup A\) exists.

\(A\) is bounded above: \(\forall x \in A\), \(x^2 < 2\). Then, \(x^2 < 4\).
We know that \(x \geq 2 \Rightarrow x^2 \geq 4\), so taking the contrapositive gives us \(x < 2\). Thus, \(2\) is an upper bound of \(A\).
\(A\) is nonempty: \(1 \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(1^2 = 1 < 2\). Then \(1 \in A\).

Let \(r := \sup A\). We then show that \(r^2 = 2\).

(\(r^2 \geq 2\)):
Take a positive number \(s\) s.t. \(s^2 < 2\). We wish to find an \(h > 0\) s.t. \((s+h)^2 < 2\). Since \(2 - s^2 > 0\), \(\dfrac{2 - s^2}{2s+1} > 0\).
We choose \(h\) s.t. \(0 < h < \dfrac{2-s^2}{2s+1}\), and also that \(h < 1\).
Note that \[
\begin{aligned}
(s+h)^2 - s^2 &= 2sh + h^2 \\
&= h(2s+h) \\
&< h(2s+1) && [h < 1] \\
&< 2 - s^2 && \left[h < \tfrac{2-s^2}{2s+1}\right]
\end{aligned}
\] and thus \((s+h)^2 < 2\), so \(s + h \in A\).
Since we found an \(h > 0\) s.t. \(s+h \in A\), \(s < s+h \leq \sup A = r\).
Thus \(s < r \ \forall s \in A\).
Suppose \(r^2 < 2\). Then \(r \in A\), and so from the argument above, \(r < r\).
This is a contradiction. Thus, \(r^2 \geq 2\).
(\(r^2 \leq 2\)):
Take a positive number \(s\) s.t. \(s^2 > 2\). If we show that \(r < s\) for any \(s\), then \(r^2 \leq 2\).
To show the inequality, we show that for an \(h > 0\), \(s - h\) is an upper bound for \(A\), and thus \(r \leq s - h < s\). We need \((s-h)^2 > 2\) and \(s - h > 0\). Since \(s^2 - 2 > 0\), \(\dfrac{s^2-2}{2s} > 0\). We let \(h = \dfrac{s^2-2}{2s}\).
I: \(\displaystyle s - h = s - \frac{s^2-2}{2s} = \frac{s}{2} + \frac{1}{s} > 0\)
II: \[
\begin{aligned}
s^2 - (s-h)^2 &= 2sh - h^2 \\
&< 2sh \\
&= s^2 - 2 && \left[h = \tfrac{s^2-2}{2s}\right]
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, \((s-h)^2 > 2\).
If \(x \geq s - h\), then \(x^2 \geq (s-h)^2 > 2\), so \(x \notin A\). Thus, \(s - h\) is an upper bound of \(A\).
Since we showed both inequalities, \(r^2 = 2\).

Finally, we show Uniqueness. Suppose \(s \in \mathbb{R}\) s.t. \(s^2 = 2\) and \(s > 0\).
Then, \(s^2 = r^2\). However, if \(s < r\) then \(s^2 < r^2\), and if \(r < s\) then \(r^2 < s^2\). Thus, \(s = r\). \(\square\)


Theorem 2.1 (Archimedean Property) If \(x, y \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(x > 0\), then there exists an \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) s.t. \(nx > y\).


Proof. This is equivalent to stating that for every real number \(t := \frac{y}{x}\), \(\exists\, n \in \mathbb{N}\) s.t. \(n > t\). This is equivalently stating that \(\mathbb{N} \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) is not bounded above.
Suppose for contradiction that \(\mathbb{N}\) is bounded above. Let \(b = \sup \mathbb{N}\). \(b - 1\) cannot be an upper bound for \(\mathbb{N}\). Then, \(\exists\, m \in \mathbb{N}\) s.t. \(m > b - 1\). Then, \(m + 1 > b\). But \(m + 1 \in \mathbb{N}\), so \(b\) is not an upper bound for \(\mathbb{N}\).
[We utilize the LUB property of \(\mathbb{R}\) for the existence of \(\sup \mathbb{N}\).]


Theorem 2.2 (Density of \(\mathbb{Q}\)) If \(x, y \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(x < y\), then there exists a \(q \in \mathbb{Q}\) s.t. \(x < q < y\).


Proof. 

  
  
  
  
  
  
  \(\frac{m-1}{n}\)
  \(\frac{m}{n}\)
  \(\frac{m+1}{n}\)
  \(x\)
  \(y\)

Assume that \(x \geq 0\). Note that \(y - x > 0\). By the Archimedean property, \(\exists\, n \in \mathbb{N}\) s.t. \(y - x > \frac{1}{n}\).
Define \(A = \{k \in \mathbb{N} : k > nx\}\). By AP, \(A\) is non-empty. By WOP, \(A\) has a least element \(m\).
\(m > nx \Rightarrow x < \frac{m}{n}\).
\(m - 1 \notin A\), so \(m - 1 \leq nx \Rightarrow m \leq nx + 1\).
On the other hand, from \(n(y-x) > 1\) we have \(ny > 1 + nx\).
Thus, \(ny > m \Rightarrow y > \frac{m}{n}\). We take \(q = \frac{m}{n}\).
For \(x < 0\), if \(y > 0\) then \(q = 0\). If \(y \leq 0\), then we find \(r \in \mathbb{Q}\) s.t. \(-y < r < -x\) and let \(q = -r\). \(\square\)


Triangle Inequality: \(|x + y| \leq |x| + |y|\)
Reverse Triangle Inequality: \(\big||x| - |y|\big| \leq |x - y|\)

Proof. \(|x| = |x - y + y| \leq |x - y| + |y|\) \[
\begin{aligned}
&\Rightarrow |x| - |y| \leq |x - y| \quad \text{(i)}. \text{ Similarly,} \\
&\phantom{\Rightarrow{}} |y| - |x| \leq |x - y| \\
&\Rightarrow -(|x| - |y|) \leq |x - y| \\
&\Rightarrow |x| - |y| \geq -|x - y| \quad \text{(ii)}.
\end{aligned}
\] Thus, \(-|x - y| \leq |x| - |y| \leq |x - y|\) \[
\Rightarrow \big||x| - |y|\big| \leq |x - y|
\] \(\square\)



Theorem 2.3 (Cantor) \(\mathbb{R}\) is uncountable.

title: 3  Sequences and Series
text:
3.1 Sequences
Cauchy sequences are bounded and convergent.

title: 3  Sequences and Series
text:
Definition 3.1 (Convergence) \(x_n \to x\) if \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\), \(\exists\, N \in \mathbb{N}\) s.t. \(\forall n \geq N\), \(|x_n - x| \leq \varepsilon\).


Theorem 3.2 (Monotone Convergence) A monotone sequence \(\{x_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}\) is bounded if and only if it is convergent.
If \(\{x_n\}\) is increasing then \(\lim x_n = \sup\{x_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}\).
If \(\{x_n\}\) is decreasing then \(\lim x_n = \inf\{x_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}\).


Proof. Consider a monotone increasing sequence \(\{x_n\}\) that is bounded.
Let \(s := \sup\{x_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}\).
Let \(\varepsilon > 0\). Since \(s\) is the supremum, \(s - \varepsilon\) is not a UB, so \(\exists\, M \in \mathbb{N}\) s.t. \(x_M > s - \varepsilon\). As \(\{x_n\}\) is increasing, \(\forall n \geq M\), \(x_n > s - \varepsilon\).
Then, \(\forall n \geq M\), \(|x_n - s| = s - x_n < \varepsilon\). Thus, \(x_n \to s\).
The inverse direction of convergent \(\Rightarrow\) bounded is true for sequences in general. \(\square\)


Definition 3.3 (liminf, limsup) limsup: \[
\limsup_{n\to\infty} x_n := \lim_{n\to\infty} \sup\{x_k : k \geq n\} = \inf_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \sup\{x_k : k \geq n\}
\]
liminf: \[
\liminf_{n\to\infty} x_n := \lim_{n\to\infty} \inf\{x_k : k \geq n\} = \sup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \inf\{x_k : k \geq n\}.
\]


Theorem 3.4 If \(\{x_n\}\) is bounded, then it has a subsequence that converges to \(\limsup x_n\) and a subsequence that converges to \(\liminf x_n\).


Proof (for limsup). Define \(a_n := \sup\{x_k : k \geq n\}\). Write \(x := \limsup\limits_{n\to\infty} x_n = \lim\limits_{n\to\infty} a_n\).
We define the subsequence inductively.
Let \(n_1 := 1\). Suppose \(n_1, n_2, \dots, n_{k-1}\) are already defined. Then, we pick an \(m \geq n_{k-1} + 1\) s.t. \(a_{(n_{k-1}+1)} - x_m < \frac{1}{k}\).
Such an \(m\) exists because \(a_{(n_{k-1}+1)} = \sup\{x_k : k \geq n_{k-1} + 1\}\), and so if no such \(m\) existed then the supremum would have been lower.
Let \(n_k := m\). Then, \(\{n_k\}\) is increasing, and \(\{x_{n_k}\}\) is a subsequence of \(\{x_n\}\).
WTS \(x_{n_k} \to x\). \(\forall k \geq 2\), \(a_{(n_{k-1}+1)} \geq a_{n_k}\), since \(n_k \geq n_{k-1} + 1\), and taking the supremum of a larger set can only result in a higher number. Also, \(a_{n_k} \geq x_{n_k}\) since the supremum is taken over a set containing \(x_{n_k}\).
Thus, \(\forall k \geq 2\), \[
\begin{aligned}
|a_{n_k} - x_{n_k}| &= a_{n_k} - x_{n_k} \\
&\leq a_{(n_{k-1}+1)} - x_{n_k} \\
&< \tfrac{1}{k} && [\text{by definition of } n_k]
\end{aligned}
\]
Let \(\varepsilon > 0\). As \(a_n \to x\), the subsequence \(a_{n_k} \to x\). Thus, \(\exists\, M_1 \in \mathbb{N}\) s.t. \(\forall k \geq M_1\), \(|a_{n_k} - x| < \varepsilon/2\).
Furthermore, let \(M_2 \in \mathbb{N}\) s.t. \(\frac{1}{M_2} \leq \varepsilon/2\).
Then, let \(M := \max\{M_1, M_2, 2\}\). \(\forall k \geq M\), \[
\begin{aligned}
|x - x_{n_k}| &= |a_{n_k} - x_{n_k} + x - a_{n_k}| \\
&\leq |a_{n_k} - x_{n_k}| + |a_{n_k} - x| \\
&< \frac{1}{k} + \varepsilon/2 \\
&\leq \frac{1}{M_2} + \varepsilon/2 \\
&\leq \varepsilon
\end{aligned}
\] \(\square\)


Theorem 3.5 (Bolzano-Weierstrass) If \(\{x_n\}\) is bounded, then there exists a convergent subsequence \(\{x_{n_i}\}\).


Proof. Following the previous thm on bounded sequences, we know that there exist subsequences that converge to \(\limsup x_n\) and \(\liminf x_n\). \(\square\)
[Note that this proof only applies to \(\mathbb{R}\), while Bolzano-Weierstrass applies to \(\mathbb{R}^n\).]


Proof (Alternate). As the sequence is bounded, there exist two numbers \(a_1 < b_1\) s.t. \(a_1 \leq x_n \leq b_1\) \(\forall n \in \mathbb{N}\). The idea of the proof is that we will define a subsequence \(\{x_{n_i}\}\) and two sequences \(\{a_i\}\) and \(\{b_i\}\), such that \(\{a_i\}\) is monotone increasing, \(\{b_i\}\) is monotone decreasing, \(a_i \leq x_{n_i} \leq b_i\), and such that \(\lim a_i = \lim b_i\). Then, by squeeze theorem \(\{x_{n_i}\}\) converges.
We define the sequences inductively. We will define the sequences so that for all \(i\), we have \(a_i < b_i\) and \(x_n \in [a_i, b_i]\) for infinitely many \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). As stated above, \(a_1\) and \(b_1\) bound the entire sequence.
We take \(n_1 = 1\), i.e. \(x_{n_1} = x_1\).
Induction: Suppose that up to some \(k \in \mathbb{N}\), we have defined the subsequence \(x_{n_1}, \dots, x_{n_k}\), and the sequences \(a_1, \dots, a_k\) & \(b_1, \dots, b_k\). Let \(y = \frac{a_k + b_k}{2}\), so \(a_k < y < b_k\).
If there exists infinitely many \(j \in \mathbb{N}\) s.t. \(x_j \in [a_k, y]\), then set \(a_{k+1} = a_k\) and \(b_{k+1} = y\), and pick the next element in the subsequence with \(n_{k+1} > n_k\) such that \(x_{n_{k+1}} \in [a_k, y]\). Consider if there doesn’t exist infinitely many \(j \in \mathbb{N}\) s.t. \(x_j \in [a_k, y]\). But then since there are infinitely many elements of \(\{x_n\}\) in \([a_k, b_k]\) from the inductive hypothesis, there must be infinitely many \(j \in \mathbb{N}\) s.t. \(x_j \in [y, b_k]\). Then, let \(a_{k+1} = y\), \(b_{k+1} = b_k\), and pick \(n_{k+1} > n_k\) s.t. \(x_{n_{k+1}} \in [y, b_k]\).
This sequence satisfies all requirements, all that is left is to prove that \(\{a_i\}\) and \(\{b_i\}\) converge to the same limit (the limits exist by monotone convergence).
\(b_i - a_i\) is cut in half each step of the construction, i.e. \(b_{i+1} - a_{i+1} = \frac{b_i - a_i}{2}\). Tracing back to the first step, \(b_i - a_i = \frac{b_1 - a_1}{2^{i-1}}\).
Let \(x = \lim a_i = \sup\{a_i\}\) and \(y = \lim b_i = \inf\{b_i\}\). Since \(a_i < b_i\) \(\forall i\), \(x \leq y\). Also, as the distance between \(a_i\) & \(b_i\) is always decreasing, \(\forall i\), \(y - x \leq b_i - a_i = \frac{b_1 - a_1}{2^{i-1}}\). For all \(\varepsilon > 0\), we can always find \(i \in \mathbb{N}\) s.t. \(\frac{b_1 - a_1}{2^{i-1}} \leq \varepsilon\). Thus, \(y - x = 0\), and the 2 limits are equal. \(\square\)


Definition 3.6 (Cauchy sequence) A sequence \(\{x_n\}\) is a cauchy sequence if \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\) \(\exists\, N \in \mathbb{N}\) s.t. \(\forall n, k \geq N\), \(|x_n - x_k| < \varepsilon\).

title: 3  Sequences and Series
text:
3.2 Series

Definition 3.7 (Series) A series converges if the sequence of its partial sums converges. \[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} x_n = \lim_{k\to\infty} \sum_{n=1}^{k} x_n
\]


Example 3.8 (Geometric Series)  

partial sum: \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{k-1} r^n = \frac{1 - r^k}{1 - r}\)
Convergence: \(-1 < r < 1\), \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} r^n = \frac{1}{1-r}\).



Example 3.9 (P-Series) \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^p}\)

\(p > 1\): converges
\(p \leq 1\): diverges



Definition 3.10 (Cauchy series) A series whose sequence of partial sums form a cauchy sequence.


Proposition 3.11 A series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} x_n\) is convergent if and only if \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\), \(\exists\, M \in \mathbb{N}\) s.t. \(\forall n \geq M\) and \(k > n\), \(\left|\sum_{i=n+1}^{k} x_i\right| < \varepsilon\).


Proof. All convergent series are cauchy. Then, we have an \(M \in \mathbb{N}\) s.t. \(\forall n, k \geq M\), \(k > n\), \[
\left| \sum_{i=1}^{k} x_i - \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \right| < \varepsilon
\] \[
\iff \left| \sum_{i=n+1}^{k} x_i \right| < \varepsilon.
\] \(\square\)


Definition 3.12 (Absolute convergence) \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} |x_n|\) converges.


Proof (of Absolute Convergence \(\Rightarrow\) Convergence). If \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} |x_n|\) converges, then it is Cauchy. Then, \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\), \(\exists\, M \in \mathbb{N}\) s.t. \(\forall k \geq M\) and \(n > k\), \(\left|\sum_{i=k+1}^{n} |x_i|\right| < \varepsilon\).
Since all the terms \(\geq 0\), \(\sum_{i=k+1}^{n} |x_i| < \varepsilon\). We then go back to the original series: \[
\left| \sum_{i=k+1}^{n} x_i \right| \leq \sum_{i=k+1}^{n} |x_i| < \varepsilon.
\] Thus, the original series is cauchy, and is convergent. \(\square\)


3.2.1 Tests for convergence

Comparison test.
Ratio test \[
R = \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{|x_{n+1}|}{|x_n|}
\]
Root test \[
R = \limsup_{n\to\infty} |x_n|^{1/n}
\]
\[
\begin{cases}
R < 1 : \text{converges absolutely} \\
R > 1 : \text{diverges}
\end{cases}
\]
Alternating Series test
Let \(\{x_n\}\) be a monotone decreasing sequence of positive real numbers such that \(\lim\limits_{n\to\infty} x_n = 0\). Then \[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (-1)^n x_n \text{ converges.}
\]

title: 3  Sequences and Series
text:
3.3 Power Series
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n (x - x_0)^n \quad \text{for } x_0 \in \mathbb{R} \text{ is power series about } x_0.
\]
Finding radius of convergence: \[
L = \limsup_{n\to\infty} \left| a_n (x - x_0)^n \right|^{1/n} = \limsup |a_n|^{1/n} \cdot |x - x_0|
\] \[
L < 1 \iff |x - x_0| < \left[ \limsup |a_n|^{\frac{1}{n}} \right]^{-1}.
\]
Radius of convergence \(\displaystyle R = \frac{1}{\limsup |a_n|^{1/n}}\) \(\square\)

title: 4  Continuous Functions
text:
4.1 Limits of functions
Previously, we defined limits in the context of sequences. Now we extend the definition to functions. Given a function \(f : S \to \mathbb{R}\), we want to see how \(f(x)\) behaves as \(x\) approaches a certain point.
In order for \(x \in S\) to approach a certain point, there must be elements of \(S\) arbitrarily near the point. We can only talk about the limit of functions at such points, called cluster points.
i.e. for any arbitrary \(\varepsilon > 0\), the \(\varepsilon\)-neighborhood of \(x\), discarding \(x\) itself, has elements of \(S\) in it. Note that this is equivalent to saying that the \(\varepsilon\)-neighborhood of \(x\), \((x - \varepsilon, x + \varepsilon)\), contains infinitely many elements of \(S\), since for any \(y \in S\) that satisfies \(0 < |x - y| < \varepsilon\), we can take another \(\varepsilon\) less than \(|x - y|\) to find another point.
Now that we have defined cluster points, we can define the limit of a function \(f(x)\) as \(x\) approaches a cluster point \(c\).
We can also relate the limit of a function with sequential limits using the sequential limit definition of cluster points:
This allows us to apply the properties of sequential limits to \(\{f(x_n)\}\),

title: 4  Continuous Functions
text:
Definition 4.1 (Cluster points) Given a set \(S \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), a number \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) is called a cluster point of \(S\) if \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\), \[
((x - \varepsilon, x + \varepsilon) \setminus \{x\}) \cap S \neq \varnothing.
\]



Remark. 

A cluster point of \(S\) does not need to be in \(S\).
By this way of defining cluster points, we can relate them to the limit of a sequence that approaches the point.



Proposition 4.2 \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) is a cluster point of \(S\) if and only if \(\exists\) a convergent sequence \(\{x_n\}\) s.t. \(\forall n \in \mathbb{N}\), \(x_n \neq x\) and \(x_n \in S\), and \(\lim x_n = x\).


Proof. (\(\Rightarrow\)) If \(x\) is a cluster point of \(S\), then \(((x - \frac{1}{n}, x + \frac{1}{n}) \setminus \{x\}) \cap S\) is always non empty. Then, we can repeatedly pick \(x_n\) from the set so that \(|x - x_n| < \frac{1}{n} \Rightarrow x_n \to x\).
(\(\Leftarrow\)) If such a sequence \(\{x_n\}\) exists and \(x_n \to x\). Then \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\), \(\exists\, M \in \mathbb{N}\) s.t. \(|x_M - x| < \varepsilon \Rightarrow x_M \in (x - \varepsilon, x + \varepsilon) \cap S \setminus \{x\}\). \(\square\)







NoteExamples of cluster points




Let \(C(S)\) denote the cluster points of \(S\)
\(C(\mathbb{Q}) = \mathbb{R}\)
\(C(\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}) = \mathbb{R}\)
\(C([0,1]) = [0,1]\)
\(C((0,1)) = [0,1]\)
\(C(\{\frac{1}{n} : n \in \mathbb{N}\}) = \{0\}\)
\(C(\mathbb{N}) = \varnothing\)





Definition 4.3 (Limit of a function) Let \(f : S \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function and \(c\) be a cluster point of \(S \subseteq \mathbb{R}\). Suppose \(\exists\, L \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\), \(\exists\, \delta > 0\) s.t. if \(x \in S \setminus \{c\}\) and \(|x - c| < \delta\), then \(|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon\).
Then, \(f(x)\) converges to \(L\) as \(x\) goes to \(c\), i.e. \[
\lim_{x \to c} f(x) := L.
\]



Lemma 4.4 \(f(x) \to L\) as \(x \to c\) if and only if for every sequence \(\{x_n\}\) where \(x_n \in S \setminus \{c\}\) and \(x_n \to c\), \(\{f(x_n)\}\) converges to \(L\).

title: 4  Continuous Functions
text:
4.2 Continuous functions
We first define continuity at a point.

Definition 4.5 \(f : S \to \mathbb{R}\) is continuous at \(c\) if \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\), \(\exists\, \delta > 0\) s.t. whenever \(x \in S\) and \(|x - c| < \delta\), we have \(|f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\).
If \(f\) is continuous \(\forall c \in S\), then \(f\) is a continuous function.


Remark. Comparison with limit definition at a point \(c\):

limit: \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\), \(\exists\, \delta > 0\) s.t. \[
0 < |x - c| < \delta \Rightarrow |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon.
\]
continuity: \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\), \(\exists\, \delta > 0\) s.t. \[
|x - c| < \delta \Rightarrow |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon.
\]
For a function to be continuous, we also have to consider its value at the point \(c\), hence we do not exclude it. Furthermore, since we are now including the point \(c\), we need \(f(x)\) to approach \(f(c)\) rather than any arbitrary \(L\).
Equivalently, continuity means that \(\lim\limits_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)\).



Proposition 4.6 I. If \(c\) is a cluster point of \(S\), then \(f\) is continuous at \(c\) if and only if \(\lim\limits_{x \to c} f(x)\) exists and is equal to \(f(c)\).
II. \(f\) is continuous at \(c\) if and only if for every sequence \(\{x_n\}\) where \(x_n \in S\) and \(x_n \to c\), \(f(x_n) \to f(c)\).
III. If \(c\) is NOT a cluster point of \(S\), then \(f\) is continuous at \(c\).


Proof (of II). (\(\Rightarrow\)) Suppose \(f\) is continuous at \(c\). Let \(\{x_n\}\) be a sequence s.t. \(x_n \in S\) and \(x_n \to c\).
Let \(\varepsilon > 0\). We take \(\delta > 0\) s.t. \(|f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\) when \(|x - c| < \delta\) by the definition of continuity. Choose \(M \in \mathbb{N}\) s.t. \(\forall n \geq M\), \(|x_n - c| < \delta\).
Then, \(\forall n \geq M\), \(|f(x_n) - f(c)| < \varepsilon \Rightarrow f(x_n) \to f(c)\).
(\(\Leftarrow\)) By contrapositive. Suppose \(f\) is not continuous at \(c\). Then, \(\exists\, \varepsilon > 0\) s.t. \(\forall \delta > 0\), \(\exists\, x \in S\) s.t. \(|x - c| < \delta\) but \(|f(x) - f(c)| \geq \varepsilon\).
We then define \(\{x_n\}\) so that \(x_n \to c\) but \(\{f(x_n)\}\) doesn’t converge to \(f(c)\). Choose \(x_n\) s.t. \(|x_n - c| < \frac{1}{n}\) and \(|f(x_n) - f(c)| \geq \varepsilon\).
Then, \(x_n \to c\), but \(|f(x_n) - f(c)| \geq \varepsilon\) \(\forall n \in \mathbb{N}\), so it doesn’t converge to \(f(c)\).


Example 4.7 Continuity of \(f(x) = 1/x\) on \((0, \infty)\) using continuity of algebraic operations, using prop II.
Let \(c \in (0, \infty)\). Let \(\{x_n\}\) be a sequence in \((0, \infty)\) s.t. \(x_n \to c\). Then, \[
f(c) = \frac{1}{c} = \frac{1}{\lim x_n} = \lim \frac{1}{x_n} = \lim f(x_n)
\] Hence, \(f(x_n) \to f(c)\). \(\square\)


4.2.1 Dirichlet function
\[
f(x) := \begin{cases} 1, & x \in \mathbb{Q} \\ 0, & x \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q} \end{cases}
\]
The dirichlet function is discontinuous at all \(c \in \mathbb{R}\).

Proof. If \(c \in \mathbb{Q}\), then we take a sequence \(\{x_n\}\) of irrational numbers in \(\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\lim x_n = c\). Then, \(f(x_n) = 0\), so \(\lim f(x_n) = 0\), but \(f(c) = 1\).
We do a similar but opposite construction for \(c \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}\).
The sequence can simply be chosen with \(x_n\) satisfying \(c < x_n < c + \frac{1}{n}\), due to density of \(\mathbb{Q}\) in \(\mathbb{R}\). \(\square\)

title: 4  Continuous Functions
text:
4.3 Theorems on Continuous functions

Theorem 4.8 Continuous functions on closed and bounded intervals are bounded.
Let \(f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be continuous. Then \(\exists\, C > 0\) s.t. \(|f(x)| \leq C\) \(\forall x \in [a,b]\).


Proof. 

We define a sequence \(\{x_n\}\) s.t. \(\forall n \in \mathbb{N}\), choose \(x_n \in [a,b]\) s.t. \(|f(x_n)| > n\).
Since \(\{x_n\}\) is bounded, by B-W there exists a convergent subsequence \(\{x_{n_k}\}\). Let \(x_{n_k} \to \ell \in [a,b]\).
By definition of continuity, \(x_{n_k} \to \ell\), so \(f(x_{n_k}) \to f(\ell)\).
Then, \(f(x_{n_k})\) is convergent and also bounded. Let \(B\) be a bound for \(f(x_{n_k})\), i.e. \(|f(x_{n_k})| \leq B\) \(\forall k\).
We arrive at a contradiction with the constructed sequence \(\{x_n\}\). Since \(\{x_{n_k}\}\) is a subsequence, it still has the property that \(|f(x_{n_k})| > n_k\). However \(n_k\) is not bounded, so if we choose \(n_k > B\), then \[
B < n_k < |f(x_{n_k})| \leq B,
\] which is a contradiction. \(\square\)



Theorem 4.9 (Extreme Value Theorem) A continuous function \(f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}\) achieves both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on \([a,b]\).


Note: \(f\) achieves an absolute maximum at \(c \in S\) if \(f(x) \leq f(c)\) \(\forall x \in S\). [similar for absolute minimum].


Theorem 4.10 (Intermediate Value Theorem) Let \(f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be continuous. Suppose \(y \in \mathbb{R}\) s.t. \(f(a) < y < f(b)\) or \(f(a) > y > f(b)\). Then, \(\exists\, c \in [a,b]\) s.t. \(f(c) = y\).

i.e. A continuous function on a closed interval achieves all the values between the values at the endpoints.

Corollary 4.11 Define \(\sup f\) as \(\sup(\operatorname{range}(f))\) and \(\inf f\) as \(\inf(\operatorname{range}(f))\). Then, \[
\operatorname{range}(f) = [\inf f, \sup f].
\]


Proof. This is proven by letting \(a = x_{\min}\) and \(b = x_{\max}\) in the intermediate value theorem. \(\square\)

title: 4  Continuous Functions
text:
4.4 Uniform Continuity

Definition 4.12 Let \(f : S \to \mathbb{R}\). Suppose that for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there exists a \(\delta > 0\) s.t. whenever \(x, c \in S\) and \(|x - c| < \delta\), then \(|f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\).
Then, \(f\) is uniformly continuous.

Comparison with continuity:

We pick a \(\delta_\varepsilon\) that works for all \(c \in S\) in the case of uniform continuity, while in continuity it depends on \(c\) and \(\varepsilon\).
Thus, uniform continuity depends on the domain.
\(\begin{cases} \text{Continuity: } \forall x,\ \forall \varepsilon\ \exists \delta \text{ s.t. } \forall c \dots \\ \text{Uniform Continuity: } \forall \varepsilon,\ \exists \delta \text{ s.t. } \forall x, c \dots \end{cases}\)


Theorem 4.13 Let \(f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be continuous. Then, \(f\) is uniformly continuous.


Proof. Contrapositive.
Suppose \(f\) is not uniformly continuous. We WTS that \(\exists\, c \in [a,b]\) s.t. \(f\) is not continuous.
By negation of uniform continuity, \(\exists\, \varepsilon > 0\), s.t. \(\forall \delta > 0\), \(\exists\, x, y \in [a,b]\) with \(|x - y| < \delta\) and \(|f(x) - f(y)| \geq \varepsilon\).
Then, for this \(\varepsilon\), since all the \(\delta\) is applicable, we let \(\delta = \frac{1}{n}\) \(\forall n \in \mathbb{N}\) and create sequences \(\{x_n\}\) and \(\{y_n\}\) s.t. \[
|x_n - y_n| < 1/n \text{ and } |f(x_n) - f(y_n)| \geq \varepsilon.
\]
By B-W, \(\exists\) a convergent subsequence \(\{x_{n_k}\}\). Let \(x_{n_k} \to c\). Since \([a,b]\) is closed, \(a \leq c \leq b\).
Consider \(\{y_{n_k}\}\), the subsequence of \(\{y_n\}\) corresponding to \(\{x_{n_k}\}\), \[
\begin{aligned}
|y_{n_k} - c| &\leq |y_{n_k} - x_{n_k}| + |x_{n_k} - c| \\
&\leq 1/n_k + |x_{n_k} - c|.
\end{aligned}
\] both terms \(\to 0\) as \(k \to \infty\), so \(y_{n_k} \to c\).
We now show that \(f\) is not continuous at \(c\): \[
\begin{aligned}
|f(x_{n_k}) - f(c)| &= |f(x_{n_k}) - f(y_{n_k}) + f(y_{n_k}) - f(c)| \\
&\geq |f(x_{n_k}) - f(y_{n_k})| - |f(y_{n_k}) - f(c)| && [\text{inverse triangle ineq.}] \\
&\geq \varepsilon - |f(y_{n_k}) - f(c)|
\end{aligned}
\] \[
\Rightarrow |f(x_{n_k}) - f(c)| + |f(y_{n_k}) - f(c)| \geq \varepsilon.
\]
At least one of \(f(x_{n_k})\) and \(f(y_{n_k})\) does not converge to \(f(c)\). Thus \(f\) is not continuous at \(c\). \(\square\)


Example 4.14 \(f(x) = x^2\) is uniformly continuous on \([0,1]\).


Proof. \[
\begin{aligned}
|f(x) - f(c)| &= |x^2 - c^2| \\
&= |x + c|\,|x - c| \\
&\leq (|x| + |c|)\,|x - c| \\
&\leq 2\,|x - c|
\end{aligned}
\] Thus, for \(\varepsilon > 0\), we take \(\delta = \varepsilon/2\).
Then, \(|x^2 - c^2| \leq 2|x - c| < 2\delta = \varepsilon\) \(\square\)


Example 4.15 \(f(x) = x^2\) is not uniformly continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\).


Proof. Suppose for contradiction that it is uniformly continuous. Then, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), \(\exists\, \delta > 0\) s.t. \(|x - c| < \delta \Rightarrow |x^2 - c^2| < \varepsilon\).
Let \(x > 0\) and \(c = x + \delta/2\).
Notice that \[
\begin{aligned}
\varepsilon > |x^2 - c^2| &= |x + c|\,|x - c| \\
&= (2x + \delta/2)\,\delta/2 \\
&= x\delta + \delta^2/4 \\
&\geq \delta x
\end{aligned}
\] Then, \(\forall x > 0\), \(x < \frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\) for the uniform continuity to hold, which contradicts the assumption that \(\delta\) holds for all \(x\). \(\square\)
